questions.question: In a 21-week pregnancy with severe abdominal pain and dyspnoea from large abdominopelvic masses, what diagnostic modalities are considered safe and most useful, and what additional information can bimanual examination and non-contrast MRI provide beyond ultrasound?

When ultrasound in pregnancy shows two large unilocular cystic masses with regular margins and peripheral vascularisation, what differential diagnoses should be prioritized, and which imaging or anatomic clues would favor cystic-degenerating leiomyoma over decidualised endometrioma or primary ovarian neoplasm?

How should a mildly elevated CA-125 level of 41.8 U/mL be interpreted in the second trimester of pregnancy, and why is a serial trend more informative than a single value when evaluating an adnexal or pelvic mass?
What pathophysiologic processes can make a pedunculated uterine leiomyoma appear as a mixed cystic-solid mass and cause pain, low-grade fever, and leakage at surgery?
What specific clinical and radiographic features in this case justified operative intervention at 21 weeks and 6 days rather than continued expectant management?
What factors would make an open longitudinal laparotomy preferable to laparoscopy for management of a symptomatic mass in the second trimester of pregnancy?
At laparotomy, why was the torsed cranial mass excised while the fixed caudal pelvic mass was intentionally left in situ?

During non-obstetric abdominal surgery in pregnancy, what intraoperative and perioperative measures should be taken to reduce maternal and fetal risk, including fetal assessment and obstetric precautions?
Why was elective caesarean delivery at 37 weeks favored over a trial of labor in this patient, and how do the size, number, and location of leiomyomas generally influence mode of delivery?
